title: Subacute CNS Infections: Tuberculous, Cryptococcal, and Viral Encephalitis

steps.tx: Bactericidal antibiotics cause explosive bacterial cell lysis, releasing endotoxins, teichoic acid, and peptidoglycans into the subarachnoid space that dramatically worsen subarachnoid inflammation and cerebral oedema. In suspected pneumococcal meningitis, administering **adjunctive dexamethasone** (ten milligrams intravenously) prior to or simultaneously with the first dose of antibiotics significantly reduces severe hearing loss, neurological sequelae, and overall mortality.
steps.say: Bactericidal antibiotics cause explosive bacterial lysis, releasing cell wall fragments that worsen subarachnoid inflammation and cerebral edema. In pneumococcal meningitis, administering adjunctive dexamethasone prior to or with the first antibiotic dose reduces hearing loss and overall mortality.

steps.tx: The most dangerous chronic granulomatous CNS infection in high-burden regions is **tuberculous meningitis**. Arising from rupture of a subependymal or submeningeal caseating tuberculoma (Rich focus) into the subarachnoid space, it produces thick gelatinous exudate concentrated across the basal cisterns, leading to progressive basal cranial neuropathies (cranial nerves III, VI, and VII), hydrocephalus, and obliterative endarteritis causing strokes.
steps.say: The most dangerous chronic CNS infection in high-burden regions is tuberculous meningitis. Arising from rupture of a caseating Rich focus into the subarachnoid space, it produces thick gelatinous basal exudates, causing cranial neuropathies, hydrocephalus, and obliterative endarteritis.

steps.tx: Cerebrospinal fluid in tuberculous meningitis displays a clear or xanthochromic appearance with a characteristic delicate cobweb or pellicle clot forming upon standing. Analysis demonstrates moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis (one-hundred to five-hundred cells per microlitre), markedly elevated protein (frequently two-hundred to five-hundred milligrams per decilitre), and profound hypoglycorrhachia, confirmed via GeneXpert MTB/RIF or mycobacterial culture on **Lowenstein-Jensen** media.
steps.say: Cerebrospinal fluid in tuberculous meningitis displays a characteristic spider-web clot forming upon standing. Analysis demonstrates moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis, markedly elevated protein, and low glucose, confirmed via GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay or mycobacterial culture.

rows: Clear or xanthochromic; forms cobweb pellicle clot
Spontaneous fibrin clot formation on standing
Lymphocytic pleocytosis; protein > 200 mg/dL; low glucose
Positive in 30% to 50% on serial large-volume taps
Low sensitivity; requires examining centrifuged sediment
Detects M. tuberculosis DNA and Rifampicin resistance
Rapid 2-hour automated nucleic acid amplification assay

steps.tx: The leading fungal infection of the central nervous system in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with advanced HIV infection and CD4 counts under one-hundred cells per microlitre, is **cryptococcal meningitis**. Inhalation of Cryptococcus neoformans basidiospores disseminates haematogenously to the meninges, presenting subacutely with headache, low-grade fevers, vomiting, and minimal meningism.
steps.say: The leading fungal infection of the central nervous system in immunocompromised patients with advanced HIV is cryptococcal meningitis. Inhalation of Cryptococcus neoformans basidiospores disseminates to the meninges, presenting subacutely with headache, low-grade fever, and elevated opening pressure.

steps.tx: Diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis relies on demonstrating the encapsulated yeast in cerebrospinal fluid. The historic India ink preparation demonstrates round budding yeast cells surrounded by a prominent clear halo corresponding to the polysaccharide capsule, while the **cryptococcal antigen** lateral flow assay exhibits over ninety-eight percent sensitivity and specificity in both serum and CSF.
steps.say: Diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis relies on demonstrating the encapsulated yeast in spinal fluid. India ink shows round budding yeast cells surrounded by a clear halo representing the polysaccharide capsule, while the cryptococcal antigen assay exhibits over ninety-eight percent diagnostic accuracy.

right.title: Cryptococcal Antigen (CrAg)
points: Gold standard diagnostic test in serum and CSF

steps.tx: Induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis requires a two-week regimen combining intravenous liposomal **amphotericin B** and oral flucytosine, followed by high-dose oral fluconazole consolidation. Because capsular polysaccharide aggregates plug arachnoid villi, extremely elevated opening pressures exceeding twenty-five centimetres of water are common, mandating therapeutic serial daily lumbar punctures until opening pressure normalizes.
steps.say: Induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis requires a two-week regimen combining intravenous liposomal amphotericin B and oral flucytosine, followed by fluconazole consolidation. Severely elevated intracranial pressure is common, mandating therapeutic serial daily lumbar punctures.

nodes.label: Induction: Liposomal Amphotericin B + Flucytosine (2 wk)
Serial Lumbar Punctures (Keep ICP < 20 cm H2O)

steps.tx: The most common identifiable cause of fatal sporadic viral encephalitis in immunocompetent individuals is **herpes simplex encephalitis** (HSE), caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). Patients present acutely with fever, headache, altered consciousness, focal seizures, behavioural disinhibition, and prominent olfactory hallucinations or aphasia, reflecting intense necrotising inflammation.
steps.say: The most common identifiable cause of sporadic viral encephalitis in immunocompetent individuals is herpes simplex encephalitis, caused by HSV-1. Patients present with fever, headache, focal seizures, behavioural changes, and aphasia, reflecting necrotising parenchymal inflammation.

rows: Severe encephalitis with focal necrosis, seizures, aphasia
Lymphocytic (10 to 500 / uL) with RBCs present
CSF Gram stain, bacterial culture, BioFire PCR

steps.tx: Herpes simplex encephalitis exhibits a striking, pathognomonic anatomical predilection for the limbic cortex, selectively destroying the inferior and medial temporal lobe and orbital frontal cortex, visible on MRI as asymmetric hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR sequences. Immediate empiric intravenous **acyclovir** (ten milligrams per kilogram every eight hours for fourteen to twenty-one days) must be administered without delay.
steps.say: Herpes simplex encephalitis exhibits a pathognomonic predilection for the medial temporal lobe and orbital frontal cortex, seen on MRI as asymmetric hyperintensities on FLAIR sequences. Immediate empiric intravenous acyclovir must be administered without waiting for PCR results.
